metadata.title: Compressing Neural Language Models by Sparse Word Representations
metadata.authors: Yunchuan Chen, Lili Mou, Yan Xu, Ge Li, Zhi Jin
metadata.notes: Paper contains ZERO theorem-like LaTeX environments (no \newtheorem at all). Every node is a prose promotion or an equation/table/itemize span; confidences are scored accordingly (0.6-0.85).

nodes.name: \Embedding{} subnet
nodes.statement: The \Embedding{} subnet maps a word to a dense vector, representing some abstract features of the word \cite{word2vec}. Note that this subnet usually accepts a list of words (known as history or context words) and outputs a sequence of word embeddings.
differentia: maps a word to a dense vector, representing some abstract features of the word
accepts a list of words (known as history or context words) and outputs a sequence of word embeddings
nodes.origin_citation: Mikolov et al. (word2vec); Bengio et al. (NLM)

nodes.name: \Encoding{} subnet
nodes.statement: The \Encoding{} subnet encodes the history of a target word into a dense vector (known as \textit{context} or \textit{history} representation). We may either leverage FFNNs \cite{NLM} or RNNs \cite{RNNLM} as the \Encoding{} subnet, but RNNs typically yield a better performance \cite{Sundermeyer:2015gj}.
differentia: encodes the history of a target word into a dense vector (known as \textit{context} or \textit{history} representation)
nodes.origin_citation: Bengio et al. (NLM); Mikolov et al. (RNNLM); Sundermeyer et al. 2015

nodes.name: \Prediction{} subnet
nodes.statement: The \Prediction{} subnet outputs a distribution of target words as \begin{align} p(w = w_i|h) = &\dfrac{\exp(s(h, w_i))} {\sum_j \exp(s(h, w_j))}, \\ s(h, w_i) = & \trans{\vector{W}_i} \vector{h} + b_i, \end{align} where $\vector{h}$ is the vector representation of context/history $h$, obtained by the \Encoding{} subnet. $\vector{W} = (\vector{W}_1, \vector{W}_2, \dots, \vector{W}_V) \in \mathbb{R}^{C\times V}$ is the \textit{output weights} of \Prediction; $\vector{b} = (b_1, b_2, \dots, b_V) \in \mathbb{R}^{C}$ is the bias (the prior). $s(h, w_i)$ is a scoring function indicating the degree to which the context $h$ matches a target word $w_i$. ($V$ is the size of vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$; $C$ is the dimension of context/history, given by the \Encoding{} subnet.)
nodes.statement_short: The output subnet turns a context vector $\vector{h}$ into a softmax distribution over the vocabulary via per-word score vectors $\vector{W}_i$ and biases $b_i$.
differentia: outputs a distribution of target words
$s(h, w_i)$ is a scoring function indicating the degree to which the context $h$ matches a target word $w_i$

nodes.name: Base set $\mathcal{B}$ and uncommon set $\mathcal{C}$
nodes.statement: We split the vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$ into two disjoint subsets ($\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$). The first subset $\mathcal{B}$ is a base set, containing a fixed number of common words (8k in our experiments). $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{V}\backslash \mathcal{B}$ is a set of uncommon words. We would like to use $\mathcal{B}$'s word embeddings to encode $\mathcal{C}$'s.
differentia: containing a fixed number of common words (8k in our experiments)
$\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{V}\backslash \mathcal{B}$ is a set of uncommon words

nodes.name: sparse code
nodes.statement: Following most work in the literature \cite{sparse,sparse2}, we represent each uncommon word with a sparse, linear combination of common ones' embeddings. The sparse coefficients are called a \textit{sparse code} for a given word.
differentia: a sparse, linear combination of common ones' embeddings

nodes.name: natural sparse code of a base word
nodes.statement: Each word in $\mathcal{B}$ has a natural sparse code (denoted as $\vector{x}$): it is a one-hot vector with $B$ elements, the $i$-th dimension being on for the $i$-th word in $\mathcal{B}$.
differentia: the $i$-th dimension being on for the $i$-th word in $\mathcal{B}$

nodes.name: fitting loss
nodes.statement: The first term (called \textit{fitting loss} afterwards) evaluates the closeness between a word's coded vector representation and its ``true'' representation $\vector{w}$, which is the general goal of sparse coding.
differentia: evaluates the closeness between a word's coded vector representation and its ``true'' representation $\vector{w}$

nodes.name: \texttt{ZRegression} layer
nodes.statement: we therefore propose a \texttt{ZRegression} layer to predict the normalization constant $Z_h$ dependent on $h$, instead of treating it as a constant. The regression layer is computed by \[ Z_h^{-1} = \exp(\trans{\vector{W}_Z}\vector{h}+b_Z), \] where $\vector{W}_Z\in \mathbb{R}^{C}$ and $b_Z\in \mathbb{R}$ are weights and bias for \texttt{ZRegression}.
nodes.statement_short: A log-linear layer on the history vector $\vector{h}$ that predicts the context-dependent NCE normalization factor $Z_h$ instead of fixing $Z_h=1$.
differentia: to predict the normalization constant $Z_h$ dependent on $h$, instead of treating it as a constant

nodes.name: perplexity (PPL)
nodes.statement: We take perplexity as the performance measurement of a language model, which is defined by \[ \mathrm{PPL} = 2^{-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log_2 p(w_i|h_i)} \] where $N$ is the number of running words in the test corpus.
nodes.genus: performance measurement of a language model
nodes.section: 4.3 Quantitative Analysis of Compressed Language Models
nodes.origin_citation: standard perplexity measure for language models (uncited in this paper)

nodes.name: Softmax word probability
nodes.statement: p(w = w_i|h) = &\dfrac{\exp(s(h, w_i))} {\sum_j \exp(s(h, w_j))},
nodes.statement_short: Normalized softmax probability of the next word given the history representation.

nodes.name: Scoring function of the \Prediction{} subnet
nodes.statement: s(h, w_i) = & \trans{\vector{W}_i} \vector{h} + b_i,
nodes.statement_short: Score of target word $w_i$ is the inner product of its output weight vector with the context vector, plus a bias.

nodes.name: Embedding of a rare word from its sparse code
nodes.statement: For a word $w\in \mathcal{C}$, we shall learn a sparse vector $\vector{x} = (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_B)$ as the sparse code of the word. Provided that $\vector{x}$ has been learned (which will be introduced shortly), the embedding of $w$ is \begin{equation} \hat{\vector{w}} = \sum_{j=1}^B x_j \vector{U}_j = \vector{U}\vector{x}, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: A rare word's embedding is the sparse-code-weighted sum of base-word embeddings, $\hat{\vector{w}} = \vector{U}\vector{x}$.

nodes.name: Constant fitness/regularization ratio conditions
nodes.statement: Suppose $\vector{x}_t$ is the value we obtain after the update of the $t$-th step, we expect the importance of fitness and regularization remain unchanged during training. This is equivalent to \begin{align} \dfrac{\alpha_t R_1(\vector{x}_t)}{L(\vector{x}_t)} = w_\alpha &\equiv \mbox{const}, \\ \dfrac{\beta_t R_2(\vector{x}_t)}{L(\vector{x}_t)} = w_\beta &\equiv \mbox{const}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Require the two regularization-to-fitting-loss ratios to stay constant throughout training.

nodes.name: Adaptive $\alpha_t$ and $\beta_t$
nodes.statement: or \[ \alpha_t = \dfrac{L(\vector{x}_t)}{R_1(\vector{x}_t)} w_\alpha \text{ and } \beta_t = \dfrac{L(\vector{x}_t)}{R_2(\vector{x}_t)} w_\beta, \] where $w_\alpha$ and $w_\beta$ are the ratios between the regularization loss and the fitting loss. They are much easier to specify than $\alpha$ or $\beta$ in the problem~\eqref{eq:opt_sp}.
nodes.statement_short: Closed form for the adaptive weights obtained by solving the constant-ratio conditions for $\alpha_t$ and $\beta_t$.

nodes.name: Compressed output weight vector
nodes.statement: Formally, the $i$-th output weight vector is estimated by \begin{equation} \hat{\vector{W}}_i = \vector{D} \vector{x}_i, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Each target word's output weight vector is the base weight matrix times that word's sparse code.

nodes.name: Compressed output bias
nodes.statement: The biases can also be compressed as \begin{equation} \hat{b}_i = \vector{c} \vector{x}_i. \end{equation} where $\vector{x}_i$ is the sparse representation of the $i$-th word. (It is shared in the compression of weights and biases.)

nodes.name: Normalized language model probability with $Z_h$
nodes.statement: Formally, the estimated probability of the word $w_i$ with history/context $h$ is \begin{align} P(w|h; \vector{\theta}) &= \dfrac{1}{Z_h} P^0(w_i|h; \vector{\theta})\nonumber \\ &= \dfrac1{Z_h}\exp(s(w_i,h;\vector{\theta})), \end{align} where $\bm\theta$ is the parameters and $Z_h$ is a context-dependent normalization factor. $P^0(w_i|h; \vector{\theta})$ is the unnormalized probability of the $w$ (given by the SpUnnrmProb layer in Figure~\ref{fig:NCE-regression}).
nodes.statement_short: Model probability written as an unnormalized exponential score divided by a context-dependent factor $Z_h$.

nodes.name: NCE objective for one context occurrence
nodes.statement: The objective for each occurrence of context/history $h$ is \begin{align*} J(\vector{\theta}|h) = & \log \dfrac{P(w_i|h;\vector{\theta})} {P(w_i|h;\vector{\theta}) + k P_n(w_i)} + \\ & \sum_{j=1}^{k} \log \dfrac{kP_n(w_j)} {P(w_j|h;\vector{\theta}) + k P_n(w_j)}, \end{align*} where $P_n(w)$ is the probability of drawing a negative sample $w$; $k$ is the number of negative samples that we draw for each positive sample.
nodes.statement_short: Per-context NCE log-loss discriminating the true next word from $k$ noise samples.

nodes.name: Overall NCE objective
nodes.statement: The overall objective of NCE is \begin{equation*} J(\vector{\theta}) = \mathbb{E}_h [J(\vector{\theta}|h)] \approx \dfrac{1}{M} \sum_{i=1}^{M} J(\vector{\theta}|h_i), \end{equation*} where $h_i$ is an occurrence of the context and $M$ is the total number of context occurrences.
nodes.statement_short: Expected per-context NCE loss, approximated by the empirical average over all context occurrences.

nodes.name: Estimated probability by NCE with \texttt{ZRegression}
nodes.statement: Hence, the estimated probability by NCE with \texttt{ZRegression} is given by \begin{equation*}\nonumber P(w|h) = \exp(s(h,w)) \cdot \exp(\trans{\vector{W}_Z}\vector{h}+b_Z). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Word probability becomes the product of the exponentiated score and the predicted inverse normalizer.

nodes.name: Language modeling objective
nodes.statement: Language modeling aims to minimize the joint probability of a corpus \cite{NLP}.

nodes.name: Sparse code optimization objective
nodes.statement: To learn the sparse representation of a certain word $w$, we propose the following optimization objective \begin{align} \min_{\vector x}\ \ & \| \vector{Ux} - \vector{w} \|_{2}^{2} + \alpha \|\vector{x}\|_1 + \beta |\trans{\vector{1}} \vector{x} - 1| \nonumber\\ &{} + \gamma \trans{\vector{1}} \max \{\vector{0}, -\vector{x}\}, \end{align} where $\max$ denotes the component-wise maximum; $\vector{w}$ is the embedding for a rare word $w\in \mathcal{C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize reconstruction error of a rare word's embedding plus $\ell_1$, sum-to-one and nonnegativity penalties on its code.
assumptions: $\vector{w}$ is the embedding for a rare word $w\in \mathcal{C}$
conclusions: \min_{\vector x}\ \ & \| \vector{Ux} - \vector{w} \|_{2}^{2} + \alpha \|\vector{x}\|_1 + \beta |\trans{\vector{1}} \vector{x} - 1| \nonumber\\ &{} + \gamma \trans{\vector{1}} \max \{\vector{0}, -\vector{x}\},

nodes.name: Re-parametrized sparse coding problem with adaptive weights
nodes.statement: Concretely, we solve the following optimization problem, which is slightly different but closely related to the conceptual objective \eqref{eq:opt_sp}: \begin{equation} \min_{\vector{x}}\ \ L(\vector{x}) + \alpha_t R_1(\vector{x}) + \beta_t R_2(\vector{x}), \end{equation} where $L(\vector{x}) = \| \vector{Ux} - \vector{w} \|_{2}^{2}$, $R_1(\vector{x}) = \|\vector{x}\|_1$, and $R_2(\vector{x}) = |\trans{\vector{1}} \vector{x} - 1|$. $\alpha_t$ and $\beta_t$ are adaptive parameters that are resolved during training time.
nodes.statement_short: Same sparse-coding objective but with the nonnegativity term dropped and the two penalty weights adapted during training.
assumptions: $\alpha_t$ and $\beta_t$ are adaptive parameters that are resolved during training time
conclusions: \min_{\vector{x}}\ \ L(\vector{x}) + \alpha_t R_1(\vector{x}) + \beta_t R_2(\vector{x}),

nodes.name: Markov assumption of $n$-gram models
nodes.statement: Traditional $n$-gram models impose a Markov assumption that a word is only dependent on previous $n-1$ words and independent of its position.

nodes.name: Dictionary intuition for rare-word representation
nodes.statement: Our intuition is that oftentimes a word can be defined by a few other words, and that rare words should be defined by common ones. Therefore, it is reasonable to use a few common words' embeddings to represent that of a rare word.

nodes.name: Fixing $Z_h=1$ in the base model
nodes.statement: The NCE algorithm suggests to take $Z_h$ as parameters to optimize along with $\vector{\theta}$, but it is intractable for context with variable lengths or large sizes in language modeling. Following \newcite{Mnih:2012tv}, we set $Z_h=1$ for all $h$ in the base model (without \texttt{ZRegression}).
nodes.statement_short: Because per-context normalizers are intractable, the base model simply fixes $Z_h=1$.

nodes.name: Time complexity of neural LMs is dominated by normalization
nodes.statement: \textit{Time complexity.} Training neural LMs is typically time-consuming especially when the vocabulary size is large. The normalization factor in Equation~(\ref{eq:sNNLM}) contributes most to time complexity.
assumptions: especially when the vocabulary size is large
conclusions: Training neural LMs is typically time-consuming
The normalization factor in Equation~(\ref{eq:sNNLM}) contributes most to time complexity

nodes.name: Linear parameter growth of \Embedding{} and \Prediction{} subnets
nodes.statement: \textit{Memory complexity and model complexity.} The number of parameters in the \Embedding{} and \Prediction{} subnets in neural LMs increases linearly with respect to the vocabulary size, which is large (Table~\ref{tab:no.param}). As said in Section~\ref{sec:intro}, this is sometimes unfavorable in memory-restricted systems. Even with sufficient hardware resources, it is problematic because we are unlikely to fully tune these parameters.
nodes.statement_short: Embedding and output-layer parameter counts grow linearly in vocabulary size, which is both memory-hungry and hard to train.
assumptions: the vocabulary size, which is large
conclusions: The number of parameters in the \Embedding{} and \Prediction{} subnets in neural LMs increases linearly with respect to the vocabulary size
this is sometimes unfavorable in memory-restricted systems
it is problematic because we are unlikely to fully tune these parameters

nodes.name: Sparse codes can be shared between \Embedding{} and \Prediction{}
nodes.statement: We claim that it is reasonable to share the same set of sparse codes to represent word vectors in \Embedding{} and the output weights in the \Prediction{} subnet.
assumptions: Without loss of generality, we let $\vector{D} = \vector{W}_{:,1:B}$ be the output weights of $B$ base target words, and $\vector{c} = \vector{b}_{1:B}$ be bias of the $B$ target words.
as the values of $\bm W$ and $\bm b$ are unknown before the training of LM, we cannot obtain their sparse codes in advance
conclusions: it is reasonable to share the same set of sparse codes to represent word vectors in \Embedding{} and the output weights in the \Prediction{} subnet

nodes.name: Parameter count independent of vocabulary size
nodes.statement: In the above model, we have managed to compressed a language model whose number of parameters is irrelevant to the vocabulary size.
conclusions: a language model whose number of parameters is irrelevant to the vocabulary size

nodes.name: Instability when the true normalization factor is far from 1
nodes.statement: Although setting $Z_h$ to 1 generally works well in our experiment, we find that in certain scenarios, the model is unstable. Experiments show that when the true normalization factor is far away from 1, the cost function may vibrate.
assumptions: when the true normalization factor is far away from 1
conclusions: the model is unstable
the cost function may vibrate

nodes.name: Learned sparse codes are meaningful
nodes.statement: The qualitative analysis demonstrates that our approach can indeed learn a sparse code of a word, and that the codes are meaningful.
conclusions: our approach can indeed learn a sparse code of a word, and that the codes are meaningful

nodes.name: LSTM-based LMs outperform LBL5 and KN3
nodes.statement: As we see, LSTM-based LMs significantly outperform the log-bilinear model as well as the backoff 3-gram LM, even if the 3-gram LM is trained on a much larger corpus with 1.6 billion words.
assumptions: even if the 3-gram LM is trained on a much larger corpus with 1.6 billion words
conclusions: LSTM-based LMs significantly outperform the log-bilinear model as well as the backoff 3-gram LM

nodes.name: Compressed LMs match LSTM-z with up to 80\% memory reduction
nodes.statement: Regarding the compression method proposed in this paper, we notice that LSTM-z$,$wb and LSTM\nobreakdash-z$,$w yield similar performance to LSTM-z. In particular, LSTM-z$,$w outperforms LSTM-z in all scenarios of different vocabulary sizes. Moreover, both LSTM-z$,$wb and LSTM-z$,$w can reduce the memory consumption by up to $80\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:para}).
nodes.statement_short: Both compressed variants keep (or improve) perplexity while cutting memory by up to 80\%.
assumptions: in all scenarios of different vocabulary sizes
conclusions: LSTM-z$,$wb and LSTM\nobreakdash-z$,$w yield similar performance to LSTM-z
LSTM-z$,$w outperforms LSTM-z in all scenarios of different vocabulary sizes
both LSTM-z$,$wb and LSTM-z$,$w can reduce the memory consumption by up to $80\%$

nodes.name: Training becomes unstable after 70\% of the dataset
nodes.statement: As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:zregression}a, the training process becomes unstable after processing 70\% of the dataset: the training loss vibrates significantly, whereas the test loss increases.
conclusions: the training process becomes unstable
the training loss vibrates significantly, whereas the test loss increases

nodes.name: Instability correlates with the $Z_h$ factor
nodes.statement: We find a strong correlation between unstableness and the $Z_h$ factor in Equation~\eqref{eq:nrm_lang_model}, i.e., the sum of unnormalized probability (Figure~\ref{fig:zregression}b).
conclusions: a strong correlation between unstableness and the $Z_h$ factor in Equation~\eqref{eq:nrm_lang_model}, i.e., the sum of unnormalized probability

nodes.name: Self-normalization tendency of the $Z_h$ factor
nodes.statement: Theoretical analysis shows that the $Z_h$ factor tends to be self-normalized even though it is not forced to \cite{Gutmann:2012tr}. However, problems would occur, should it fail.
assumptions: even though it is not forced to
conclusions: the $Z_h$ factor tends to be self-normalized
problems would occur, should it fail

nodes.name: Justification for sharing sparse codes between embeddings and output weights
nodes.statement: In a given corpus, an occurrence of a word is always companied by its context. The co-occurrence statistics about a word or corresponding context are the same. As both word embedding and context vectors capture these co-occurrence statistics \cite{Levy:2014wb}, we can expect that context vectors share the same internal structure as embeddings. Moreover, for a fine-trained network, given any word $w$ and its context $h$, the output layer's weight vector corresponding to $w$ should specify a large inner-product score for the context $h$; thus these context vectors should approximate the weight vector of $w$. Therefore, word embeddings and the output weight vectors should share the same internal structures and it is plausible to use a same set of sparse representations for both words and target-word weight vectors. As we shall show in Section~\ref{sec:experiment}, our treatment of compressing the \Prediction{} subnet does make sense and achieves high performance.
nodes.statement_short: Co-occurrence argument: embeddings and context vectors encode the same statistics, and output weight vectors approximate context vectors, so one code set suffices.

nodes.name: Word and context share co-occurrence statistics
nodes.statement: In a given corpus, an occurrence of a word is always companied by its context. The co-occurrence statistics about a word or corresponding context are the same.
nodes.statement_short: Set up the premise that a word and its context carry identical co-occurrence statistics.

nodes.name: Context vectors share the internal structure of embeddings
nodes.statement: As both word embedding and context vectors capture these co-occurrence statistics \cite{Levy:2014wb}, we can expect that context vectors share the same internal structure as embeddings.
nodes.statement_short: Invoke Levy & Goldberg to transfer the shared statistics into shared internal structure.

nodes.name: Output weight vectors approximate context vectors
nodes.statement: Moreover, for a fine-trained network, given any word $w$ and its context $h$, the output layer's weight vector corresponding to $w$ should specify a large inner-product score for the context $h$; thus these context vectors should approximate the weight vector of $w$.
nodes.statement_short: Large inner-product scores force the output weight vector of $w$ to be close to its context vectors.

nodes.name: Conclude that one set of sparse codes suffices
nodes.statement: Therefore, word embeddings and the output weight vectors should share the same internal structures and it is plausible to use a same set of sparse representations for both words and target-word weight vectors.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude that a single sparse-code set can serve both embeddings and output weights.

nodes.name: Compressed neural language model
nodes.statement: Based on the pre-computed sparse codes, we design our compressed language model as follows. A dense embedding is assigned to each common word; an infrequent word, on the other hand, computes its vector representation by a sparse combination of common words' embeddings. We use the long short term memory (LSTM)-based recurrent neural network (RNN) as the hidden layer of our model. The weights of the output layer are also compressed in a same way as embeddings.
nodes.statement_short: An LSTM language model in which rare words' embeddings and output weights are sparse combinations of a small set of common-word parameters.
input: A dense embedding is assigned to each common word
output: its vector representation by a sparse combination of common words' embeddings
The weights of the output layer are also compressed in a same way as embeddings

nodes.name: Assign dense embeddings to common words
nodes.statement: A dense embedding is assigned to each common word;
nodes.statement_short: Initialize a dense embedding per common (base) word.

nodes.name: Compose rare-word embeddings from sparse codes
nodes.statement: an infrequent word, on the other hand, computes its vector representation by a sparse combination of common words' embeddings.
nodes.statement_short: Compute each rare word's embedding as a sparse combination of base embeddings.

nodes.name: Encode history with an LSTM-RNN
nodes.statement: We use the long short term memory (LSTM)-based recurrent neural network (RNN) as the hidden layer of our model.
nodes.statement_short: Use an LSTM-RNN as the hidden (encoding) layer.

nodes.name: Compress the output layer weights
nodes.statement: The weights of the output layer are also compressed in a same way as embeddings.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the same sparse-code compression to the output weights.

nodes.name: Noise-contrastive estimation (NCE)
nodes.statement: NCE generates a few negative samples for each positive data sample. During training, we only need to compute the unnormalized probability of these positive and negative samples. Interested readers are referred to \cite{Gutmann:2012tr} for more information.
nodes.statement_short: Train by discriminating each true next word from a handful of sampled noise words, avoiding full-vocabulary normalization.
input: a few negative samples for each positive data sample
output: the unnormalized probability of these positive and negative samples

nodes.name: Sparse code computation procedure
nodes.statement: To obtain words' sparse codes, we chose 8k common words as the ``dictionary,'' i.e., $B=8000$. We had 2k--42k uncommon words in different settings. We first pretrained word embeddings of both rare and common words, and obtained 200d vectors $\vector{U}$ and $\vector{w}$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:opt_sp_trick}. The dimension was specified in advance and not tuned. As there is no analytic solution to the objective, we optimized it by Adam \cite{Kingma:2014us}, which is a gradient-based method. To filter out small coefficients around zero, we simply set a value to 0 if it is less than $0.015\cdot\max\{v\in\vector{x}\}$. $w_\alpha$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:alpha} was set to 1 because we deemed fitting loss and sparsity penalty are equally important. We set $w_\beta$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:beta} to 0.1, and this hyperparameter is insensitive.
nodes.statement_short: Pretrain 200d word2vec embeddings, then minimize the re-parametrized sparse-coding objective with Adam and threshold near-zero coefficients.

nodes.name: Choose the base dictionary
nodes.statement: To obtain words' sparse codes, we chose 8k common words as the ``dictionary,'' i.e., $B=8000$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix the base dictionary to the 8k most common words.

nodes.name: Pretrain 200d word embeddings
nodes.statement: We first pretrained word embeddings of both rare and common words, and obtained 200d vectors $\vector{U}$ and $\vector{w}$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:opt_sp_trick}.
nodes.statement_short: Pretrain the ``true'' embeddings that supply $\vector{U}$ and $\vector{w}$.

nodes.name: Optimize the objective with Adam
nodes.statement: As there is no analytic solution to the objective, we optimized it by Adam \cite{Kingma:2014us}, which is a gradient-based method.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the sparse-coding objective numerically with Adam.

nodes.name: Threshold near-zero coefficients
nodes.statement: To filter out small coefficients around zero, we simply set a value to 0 if it is less than $0.015\cdot\max\{v\in\vector{x}\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Zero out coefficients below 1.5\% of the code's maximum to enforce sparsity.

nodes.name: KN3
nodes.statement: \textbf{KN3}. We adopted the modified Kneser-Ney smoothing technique to train a 3-gram LM; we used the SRILM toolkit \cite{toolkit} in out experiment.
nodes.statement_short: Baseline: modified Kneser-Ney smoothed 3-gram language model trained with SRILM.

nodes.name: LBL5
nodes.statement: \textbf{LBL5}. A \textbf{L}og-\textbf{B}i\textbf{L}inear model introduced in \newcite{three}. We used 5 preceding words as context.
nodes.statement_short: Baseline: log-bilinear neural LM with a 5-word context window.

nodes.name: LSTM-s
nodes.statement: \textbf{LSTM-s}. A standard LSTM-RNN language model which is applied in \newcite{Sundermeyer:2015gj} and \newcite{visualize}. We implemented the LM ourselves based on Theano \cite{2016arXiv160502688short} and also used NCE for training.
nodes.statement_short: Baseline: standard uncompressed LSTM-RNN language model trained with NCE.
nodes.origin_citation: Sundermeyer et al. 2015; Karpathy et al. (visualize); Theano

nodes.name: LSTM-z
nodes.statement: \textbf{LSTM-z}. An LSTM-RNN enhanced with the \texttt{ZRegression} mechanism described in Section~\ref{ss:NCE}.
nodes.statement_short: Uncompressed LSTM LM plus the \texttt{ZRegression} normalization-prediction layer.

nodes.name: LSTM-z,wb
nodes.statement: \textbf{LSTM-z$,$wb}. Based on LSTM-z, we compressed word embeddings in \Embedding{} and the output weights and biases in \Prediction{}.
nodes.statement_short: Fully compressed variant: embeddings, output weights and biases all reconstructed from sparse codes.
output: word embeddings in \Embedding{} and the output weights and biases in \Prediction{}

nodes.name: LSTM-z,w
nodes.statement: \textbf{LSTM-z$,$w}. In this variant, we did not compress the bias term in the output layer. For each word in $\mathcal{C}$, we assigned an independent bias parameter.
nodes.statement_short: Compressed variant that keeps a free bias per word while compressing embeddings and output weights.
input: For each word in $\mathcal{C}$, we assigned an independent bias parameter

nodes.name: Sparse codes of \textit{algorithm}, \textit{secret}, \textit{debate}, \textit{algorithms}
nodes.statement: Figure~\ref{fig:sparse} plots the sparse codes of a few selected words. As we see, \textit{algorithm}, \textit{secret}, and \textit{debate} are common words, and each is (sparsely) coded by itself with a coefficient of 1. We further notice that a rare word like \textit{algorithms} has a sparse representation with only a few non-zero coefficient.
nodes.statement_short: Common words are coded by themselves with coefficient 1, while the rare word \textit{algorithms} gets only a few non-zero coefficients.

nodes.name: Code of \textit{algorithms} weights the base word \textit{algorithm}
nodes.statement: Moreover, the coefficient in the code of \textit{algorithms}---corresponding to the base word \textit{algorithm}---is large ($\sim\!\!0.6$), showing that the words \textit{algorithm} and \textit{algorithms} are similar. Such phenomena are also observed with \textit{secret} and \textit{debate}.
nodes.statement_short: The dominant coefficient ($\sim0.6$) of \textit{algorithms} sits on \textit{algorithm}, evidencing semantic similarity.

nodes.name: Tricks for setting the regularization hyperparameters
nodes.statement: It is difficult to determine the hyperparameters $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$. Therefore we perform several tricks. First, we drop the last term in the problem \eqref{eq:opt_sp}, but clip each element in $\vector{x}$ so that all the sparse codes are nonnegative during each update of training.
nodes.statement_short: Drop the nonnegativity penalty and enforce nonnegativity by clipping instead.

nodes.name: True embeddings are trained by word2vec and then slacked
nodes.statement: To learn the sparse codes, we first train the ``true'' embeddings by {\tt word2vec}\footnote{https://code.google.com/archive/p/word2vec} for both common words and rare words. However, these true embeddings are slacked during our language modeling.

nodes.name: Sparse codes are not tunable parameters and cost 4--8 values per word
nodes.statement: As the codes are pre-computed and remain unchanged during language modeling, they are not tunable parameters of our neural model. Considering the learned sparse codes, we need only 4--8 values for each word on average, as the codes contain 0.05--0.1\% non-zero values, which are almost negligible.
nodes.statement_short: Pre-computed codes add only 4--8 values per word and are not trained.

nodes.name: Compressed embeddings are themselves dense
nodes.statement: We would like to point out that the embedding of a word $\hat{\vector{w}}$ is not sparse because $\vector{U}$ is a dense matrix, which serves as a shared parameter of learning all words' vector representations.

nodes.name: Uncompressed-bias variant
nodes.statement: To better estimate a ``prior'' distribution of words, we may alternatively assign an independent bias to each word, i.e., $\vector{b}$ is not compressed. In this variant, the number of model parameters grows very slowly and is also negligible because each word needs only one extra parameter. Experimental results show that by not compressing the bias vector, we can even improve the performance while compressing LMs.
nodes.statement_short: Leaving one bias per word uncompressed costs almost nothing and improves performance.

nodes.name: \texttt{ZRegression} does not guarantee normalization
nodes.statement: Note that the \texttt{ZRegression} layer does not guarantee normalized probabilities. During validation and testing, we explicitly normalize the probabilities by Equation~\eqref{eq:sNNLM}.

nodes.name: Two competing effects of sparse-code compression
nodes.statement: To explain this phenomenon, we may imagine that the compression using sparse codes has two effects: it loses information, but it also enables more accurate estimation of parameters especially for rare words. When the second factor dominates, we can reasonably expect a high performance of the compressed LM.
nodes.statement_short: Compression trades information loss against better-estimated rare-word parameters.

nodes.name: \texttt{ZRegression} is generally applicable
nodes.statement: It should be mentioned that \texttt{ZRegression} is not specific to model compression and is generally applicable to other neural LMs trained by NCE.
